name: Honduras
summary: Independent in 1838 after the Central American federation broke up; the original “banana republic”; Hurricane Mitch (1998) devastated it.

knownFor.label: Bananas
knownFor.note: US fruit companies dominated the economy.

location.value: Central America, with a long Caribbean coast in the north and a short Pacific shore on the Gulf of Fonseca; about 112,000 km².

terrain.value: Mostly mountains and high valleys, with Lake Yojoa in the centre, the Caribbean lowlands in the north and the Mosquitia forests in the east.

climate.value: Tropical: hot and humid on the coasts, cooler in the mountains, with a rainy season from about May to November and frequent hurricanes.

resources.value: Fertile lowlands for bananas and palm oil, highland coffee, forests of pine and hardwoods, silver and other minerals, and shrimp.

population.value: About 10 million people (2024), up from roughly 300,000 at independence in the 1800s.

urbanisation.value: About 60% live in towns; the capital Tegucigalpa and the industrial city of San Pedro Sula are by far the largest.

disease.value: Dengue fever spread by mosquitoes, with outbreaks such as 2019; malaria and Chagas disease in rural areas.

migration.value: Large numbers have emigrated to the United States since the 1990s, especially after Hurricane Mitch (1998), to escape poverty and violence.

economicBase.value: Exports of coffee, bananas and palm oil, clothing made in maquila factories, and money sent home by emigrants (remittances).

tradeRoutes.value: Puerto Cortés on the Caribbean is the main port; San Lorenzo serves the Pacific, and highways link Honduras to its neighbours.

wealth.value: A lower-middle-income country and one of the poorer nations of the Americas, with many people living in poverty.

moneyAndTax.value: The lempira, introduced in 1931 and named after a Lenca leader who resisted the Spanish; taxes include a sales tax and income tax.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A presidential republic under the 1982 constitution, with a president, a single-chamber National Congress and a Supreme Court.

keyRulers.value: Francisco Morazán. Tiburcio Carías Andino. Xiomara Castro.

succession.value: Presidents are chosen in elections; there were long periods of military rule (1963–82), and the army removed the president in 2009.

institutions.value: The National Congress, the Supreme Court of Justice, the armed forces, and the long-rival Liberal and National parties.

stability.value: Coups and dictatorships were common until 1982; in the early 2010s it had one of the world’s highest murder rates, linked to gangs and drug trafficking.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: Army, navy and air force; the air force played a leading role in the 1969 war, and the military dominated politics for decades.

majorWars.value: The brief Football War with El Salvador (July 1969), set off by border and migration tensions during World Cup qualifying matches.

territoryChange.value: Gained the Bay Islands by a treaty with Britain (1859); border disputes with Nicaragua (1960) and El Salvador (1992) were settled at the World Court.

alliancesRivals.value: A close US ally, hosting the Soto Cano air base since the 1980s; rivalries with El Salvador and Nicaragua over borders.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: The National Autonomous University (UNAH, founded 1847) is the main university; schooling has spread, but many rural pupils leave early.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Highways link Tegucigalpa, San Pedro Sula and Puerto Cortés; old banana railways on the north coast; few roads in the Mosquitia.

religion.value: Mostly Christian: once mainly Catholic, but evangelical Protestant churches have grown fast and now include a large share of people.

languageWriting.value: Spanish is official; Garifuna, Miskito, Lenca heritage and other Indigenous languages, and English creole on the Bay Islands.

artsArchitecture.value: The ancient Maya city of Copán with its carved stelae; colonial churches such as Comayagua Cathedral; modern naïf painting.

socialStructure.value: A mestizo (mixed) majority, with Lenca, Miskito, Garifuna and other Indigenous and Afro-descendant peoples, and a small wealthy elite.

sharedIdentity.value: A shared “Catracho” national identity built around Spanish, football, Catholic and evangelical faith, and heroes such as Lempira and Morazán.

dailyLife.value: Meals of beans, corn tortillas, rice and plantains; baleadas (flour tortillas with beans and cream) are a favourite street food.

neighbours.value: Guatemala to the west, El Salvador to the south-west and Nicaragua to the south, with Belize across the Gulf of Honduras.

ideasReligions.value: Liberal reforms in the 1870s, Catholic social teaching, and the fast growth of evangelical Protestantism since the late 1900s.

colonisation.value: Part of the Spanish Empire from the 1520s until 1821, then of the Federal Republic of Central America until 1838.

riseSignals.value: Left the collapsing Federal Republic of Central America and became a separate independent republic in 1838.

peakPeriod.value: Hard to judge for a living country; return to civilian rule in 1982 and growth in the 1990s and 2000s are often seen as high points.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Still in existence as an independent republic in Central America, with its capital at Tegucigalpa.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
